claims.text: The initial materials are nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and thermally activated atomic diffusion.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic multicomponent alloys have high mixing entropy.
A strictly equiatomic composition maximizes configurational entropy relative to a slightly imbalanced composition.
A slight compositional imbalance reduces configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy increases the energetic penalty or barrier for elemental segregation and phase separation.
The entropy effect stabilizes a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Composition and annealing temperature affect phase decomposition in multicomponent alloys.
At high temperatures, thermally activated diffusion can overcome entropy stabilization and cause elemental segregation.
Equiatomic nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous single-phase solid solution over a broader high-temperature range than slightly imbalanced nanoparticles.
Slightly imbalanced nanoparticles will exhibit phase segregation and chemical demixing at a lower onset temperature than equiatomic nanoparticles.
Near 473 K, both nanoparticle sets will remain single-phase and elementally homogeneous.
An inert or reducing atmosphere minimizes external oxidation during testing.
The prediction applies only when oxidation, sintering, particle-size differences, and morphology differences are minimized.
The temperature at which diffusion overcomes entropy stabilization depends on the elemental combination and individual-metal diffusion characteristics.
Similar segregation-onset temperatures and comparable chemical instability in the two composition sets would refute a significant entropy-induced delay of segregation.
